If you want to be sure everything just works, buying a PC is a respectable move, you shouldn't have to spend any time making everything work together, getting the right drivers, navigating compatibility issues, etc.

Cost is a big issue, though... and there are PLENTY of resources to help you with building a PC, especially if you are behind on bills AND you've got lots of time until Fallout 4 hits shelves, I'd recommend you start looking for some good guides.

If you want to be sure everything just works, buying a PC is a respectable move, you shouldn't have to spend any time making everything work together

My current PC was a pre-built base which I upgraded parts from as I felt the need. It allowed me to spend more than I had on hand via a interest free payment plan. Having said that, the first one I brought home was faulty (the BD drive didn't register, was incompatible with the rest of the system).

I took it back to the store the next day and had them look at it after which they decided to replace it on the spot. For shits and giggles I asked them to test the new machine (same model) for me before I took it home. It had the same failure (since it was a hardware incompatibility and they had the same hardware).

They went to get a third of the same model and I said 'I'm going to go grab some lunch, if you find one that works I'll take it.' I left, got lunch and came back. They had removed ALL of that model pc from the showroom (iirc about 20 machines) and I had a pc worth $700 more sitting at the counter waiting for me at no extra cost. I still upgraded the GPU within 3 months because I got a deal on 2x R9 280X Black Editions (2 cards for $200, they were retailing at $350ea in Aus at the time)

Moral of the story: Even pre-builts can be major fuck ups.

That sounds like it was a pain, but the thing I take from it is that the pre-built had a guarantee on it that was solid enough to warrant $700 worth of extra parts because the original builder was a fuckup.

If you had bought all your own parts and made the same computer.... then that extra $700 and all the time would have been on you.

Because it was on a payment plan also they had already been 'paid' for the pc, so had to haul ass to fix the problem. They tried to give me another PC but I didn't like the brand of components and told them I would peruse. I checked the value of the PC they picked out then shopped for one of the same value. I think in the end it saved them a lot of trouble. They were one of Australias largest homewares stores and it was a new OEM they had started to stock. They no longer stock that OEM in any of their stores. Whoever was running the show is probably VERY pissed off at the tech who designed that system.
Building a PC is easy, I've been building my own since 2002, it just takes a little research and the right support network.

There's very little margin in PC building and, generally, PC repair. This is why most of the little computer shops have gone away; they couldn't make any money. That's no reason not to learn how to build your own PC, I'm just pointing it out in case you have aspirations of it turning into a career. By all means give it a try if you want; some people can actually make a go of it, just not as many as there used to be.

As others have mentioned there are lots of good resources on-line. It's not difficult to build your own but compared to buying pre-built you won't save much $$. You do it because you enjoy that sort of thing and because it gives you the opportunity to hand pick the parts.

Reddit had a number of pretty great subs for this sort of thing r/pcmasterracebuilds comes to mind but there were others. I haven't been there for some time so I can't speak to the quality these days. I'm not sure if voat has anything comparable yet.

Probably the hardest part is deciding which parts to get. There are few clear cut choices and everyone has an opinion so the best thing you can do is research, ask questions, and become knowledgeable. Good luck and have fun.

You need this website: pcpartspicker.com

It check compatibility of parts, gets prices from hundreds of online vendors (and often tracks down the best price for you) and can cover every component from case to peripherals to extra fans.

Or if you'd like some build suggestions give me a budget and we can talk expectations and I can throw a few builds together for you and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each one.

The one thing I will say, is you want to hit a minimum of 60fps constant. Don't be a cinematic douche, you want the frames. Frames are love, frames are life.

Most prebuilt systems are massively overpriced and underpowered. If you have the ability to fit a square peg into a square hole, then you should be able to assemble one with no problem. All that matters is finding the right parts to fit your budget.
And if you manage to fit a square peg into a round hole, you broke it.
